newsitem.title: UK: Reuter polls show UK growth peak postponed.
newsitem.headline: Reuter polls show UK growth peak postponed.

text.p: Britain's economy has not lived up to economists' expectations of a year ago, held back by weaker-than-expected manufacturing, a review of Reuters' polls showed on Friday.
But economists said the growth peak had simply been delayed until the second half of this year, with further windfalls this summer expected to fatten consumers' wallets.

In January last year an average of 38 economists in Reuters' quarterly survey of economic indicators predicted growth would reach three percent by the fourth quarter of 1996, and peak in the first quarter of 1997.
But revised figures released by the Office for National Statistics released showed gross domestic product (GDP) at 2.7 percent for quarter four of 1996.

"The pickup in the economy during the second half of last year has been slightly on the softer side of expectations, although economic activity has still been expanding at a pace above the long-term sustainable trend," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.

Economists said all the fundamentals were still in place, and Britain should see growth spurt towards the end of 1997. The most recent survey published this January pointed to a peak of 3.6 percent in the third quarter of 1997.
"Most forecasters did see a peak at the turn of the year but it's been pushed back," said Ciaran Barr, senior UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Windfall gains coming through in the summer have been bigger than people expected and should impact the consumer cycle which will help ratchet it up a gear," he said.
Many consumers will qualify for fat payouts when the likes of the Halifax, the Woolwich and Alliance and Leicester building societies convert to public companies this summer.

"People realise in 1997 that the consumer windfalls, by time they are converted to cash and people have started spending them, will not have an effect until towards the end of the year," said Andrew Schofield, senior economist at Business Strategies Ltd (BSL).
Economists also blamed slow manufacturing for delaying the growth peak, and warned that sterling's recent meteoric rise could also leave manufacturing struggling in the short term.
"Manufacturing was much slower than expected, so that pushed things out another quarter or two and we have got a problem in that sterling strength will have an impact on exports," DMG's Barr said.
But economists are not overly concerned.
"The factors that are driving the economy forward, in terms of the consumer side of things, do remain quite positive and that will feed it's way through to growth this year," added Barr.
